newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fujitsu to boost 64MB chip output as demand shifts.
newsitem.headline: Fujitsu to boost 64MB chip output as demand shifts.

text.p: Major Japanese semiconductor maker Fujitsu Ltd said on Tuesday it planned to boost output of next-generation 64-megabit memories to meet growing demand for the higher capacity chips.

But other Japanese makers said they had no immediate plans to follow suit, signalling caution about switching to the newer type of chip despite a recent fall in prices for the current mainstay memory chips.

Fujitsu said it now planned to reach an output rate of 1.5 million 64-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips per month by the end of the 1997/98 business year, up 50 percent from its previously planned one million per month by that time. The previous forecast was issued only a month ago.

"An increasing number of PCs are using 64-megabit DRAMs," a Fujitsu spokeswoman said, adding the company thinks that demand will shift from the current standard 16-megabit DRAMs to 64-megabit chips earlier than it had initially expected. She could not provide figures on current output.

A 64-megabit chip has a memory capacity four times larger than that of a 16-megabit DRAM chip. The next-generation chips are used in workstations, high-end PCs and notebook PCs. A 16-megabit DRAM chip is now the most common type for PCs.
Despite the Fujitsu move, major Japanese chip makers had no definite plans to revise 64-megabit DRAM production targets.
"We will definitely increase 64-megabit DRAM output in the future but we do not have any specific plans as regards to production after March next year," an NEC Corp spokesman said.
NEC has already said that it will be producing one million units a month by March 31, 1997.

A Mitsubishi Electric Corp spokesman said the company now makes 30,000 64-megabit DRAM chips a month and it plans to boost output to 100,000 units by the end of March 1997. "We think that our output could reach the one million level per month by the end of March 1998," the spokesman said, but he added that plans could change according to the market environment.

A Toshiba Corp spokeswoman said the company had just started mass production of that type of chip at a monthly rate of 100,000 and the company is studying market conditions before deciding its future production plans.

She said that Toshiba thought demand for 64-megabit DRAM chips would grow as large as, or slightly larger than, demand for 16-megabit DRAM chips by the end of 1997 or at the beginning of 1998. Industry sources had said that such a shift would take place after the middle of 1998, she said.
But other makers seemed to be unsure how fast demand for 64-megabit DRAM chips would grow.

"Prices of 64-megabit DRAM chips are high at the initial stage of production. Unless they can fall to a price only four to five times as expensive as 16-megabit DRAMs, a shift to 64-megabit DRAM chips would be hard," the NEC spokesman said.

Chipmakers' enthusiasm for 64-megabit DRAM chips is largely due to a sharp fall in the prices of 16-megabit DRAM chips this year and the move is not fully backed by demand, one of the chipmakers said.
The price of the 16-megabit DRAM chip was one-fifth of its January level in August, due to an unexpected slowdown in PC sales worldwide and oversupply of the chips.

Last week, however, Japan's Nihon Keizai Shimbun economic daily said overseas spot prices for 16-megabit DRAM chips were sharply recovering, reaching $12 to $15 per unit -- almost double the price at the beginning of September.
